title: 331. Matchmaker Mindset: How to Make Yourself Memorable in Any Conversation
description_html:
“Boredom is just the enemy of conversation.” 

Small talk doesn’t have to be boring. For matchmaker and dating coach Rachel Greenwald, better conversations start with a little preparation and a willingness to move beyond predictable questions toward the stories that make people memorable. In this episode of Think Fast, Talk Smart, Greenwald joins Matt Abrahams to share strategies for building stronger connections in dating, networking, and the workplace. From bridging small talk toward more meaningful topics to navigating taboo subjects and showing more vulnerability, she explains how to create conversations that bring out the best in others and ourselves.

Takeaways:

  • Better small talk starts with a little strategy. Preparing a few topics and finding natural bridges toward what makes you unique can turn routine exchanges into more memorable, meaningful interactions. 
  • Connection comes from stories, not just information. Asking questions that invite people to share experiences and emotions can reveal more than factual answers and help deepen relationships.


Activity:

  • Build a better bridge. Turn three standard small-talk questions into openings that lead somewhere more interesting. For example, instead of answering “How are you?” with “Good,” practice a response that naturally introduces a story, interest, or experience someone could ask you about.

My name's Matt Abrahams, and I teach Strategic Communication at Stanford Graduate School of Business.

Rachel is an executive fellow at Harvard Business School and a professional matchmaker and dating coach.
Rachel is an expert on communication and relationship building, not only in the dating arena, but also in the workplace.
She's here on campus at Stanford to co-teach a class with Professor Tina Seelig called Designing for Love.
Welcome, Rachel. I am so glad you decided to revisit us, and it's great to be in person this time.
Thanks for being here.
You're welcome. Thanks for having me back.
Excellent. Shall we get started?
Let's do it.
All right. The last time you were here, we talked a lot about small talk, and you gave very actionable, useful advice that I use to this day to start and to exit small talk.
The white flag approach you taught was amazing, and I really quote you often with the point that small talk is about being interested and not interesting.
And if any of you want to hear Rachel's advice on small talk, go back to episode 217.

So if those were sort of the entry-level, beginner-level small talk advice and tips, can you give us some advanced advice, black belt level small talk tips to help us better communicate and help us avoid that dread we all feel?
Yeah, everybody hates small talk because mostly it's so boring and awkward.
So I think that moving up the scale to graduate level small talk advice is really about moving from playing defense to offense.
So defense is more like coming up with good answers to basic small talk questions, which we talked about last time.
But playing offense is more about being strategic with your small talk game to help your conversation partner learn something about you that might lead to a desired goal that you have.
So this is really where your personal brand comes in, where I want you to find a bridge out of the initial stages of small talk that leads towards a topic that makes you unique and memorable.
So here's an example.
Maybe you're on a date or you're in a job interview.

You want it to go well, so you think a little bit ahead of time, "What is it that makes me unique from all the other dates that he's been on this week or all the other candidates he's interviewed this week?"
And in your case, Matt, maybe it's that being a podcast host is unique.
You know, you don't meet those hosts every day.
What I want you to do is find a bridge that is gonna take you from a basic small talk question like, "How are you?" to something that allows you to talk about being a podcast host.
So for example, if I say, "How are you?"
You might say, "Oh, I'm actually doing great today.
I just interviewed a really interesting guest on my podcast, and she told me all about organic wine."
And so now you've sort of bridged into this more interesting topic.
The key, though, is that you have to have a plan going into these type of conversations because you can't expect to just come up with something like that on the spot.
Think about if you're an athlete, you wouldn't just start exercising.
You would do some stretching and warming up before the exercise.
So all sorts of examples like this, for example, in a job interview, let's say one of the personal brand attributes that makes you unique is that you're gritty.
You, you have a lot of grit.
Maybe you walk into a job interviewer's office, and he's got a photo of himself climbing a mountain behind him on the desk.
And so you could do this bridge where you say, "Oh, I noticed that hiking photo over there.
I'm curious where that hike is because actually I just climbed Kilimanjaro this year, and it was so hard, but I did it."
And so here you're moving basic small talk into something that is strategic on your part, demonstrating your personal brand, that is grit in this case.
So what I really hear is it's about branding and bridging and how you connect those two.
And what's required there is to be a little strategic and to think in advance about what are those things that make me unique.
What advice do you have as we reflect on our personal brand?
We've had Seth Godin and Dorie Clark on the show, and they've talked about personal brand as well.
But as a matchmaker, I'm wondering if you have a specific way of thinking about brand that we could all benefit from.

I do. I mean, I think the first thing to say about personal branding is that it gets a bad reputation as being manipulative or like you're bragging or showing off if you talk about something that makes you unique or special or memorable.

So I think the first thing is you have to get that out of your head, that I think the better metaphor about personal branding is that it's almost like you're walking into a restaurant and the hostess is greeting you at the host stand, and she can either make basic small talk with you and say something like, "How are you?
Would you like a table?"
Or she could hand you a menu and essentially say, "What looks good here tonight on the menu?"
So essentially, she's focusing the initial greeting on, like, the chef's specials and what are the signature items at the restaurant.
Once you've got the right attitude about personal branding, the, the easiest shortcut to what is a personal brand is to come up with three traits or skills that makes you unique.
Seth Godin talked about this in Purple Cow, about basically how to be unique and memorable.
And I think you just come up with three things that feel authentic but also unique, kind of the Venn diagram of who you are, but what's unique about that.
So maybe you're on a date, for example, and let's say your three personal brand traits are that you're adventurous, maybe you once appeared on Shark Tank, and you're from North Dakota.
Being from North Dakota is not like being from New York or California.
It's unique. So you will pick something that is part of that personal brand and find a bridge out of small talk into focusing on something that makes you memorable.
Of course, you may not be the only one on Shark Tank.
You're not the only one who's from North Dakota.
You're not the only one who's adventurous.
But you might be the Venn diagram of those three things, and that is a great place to start when somebody on a date might say to you, "What do you do?"

You might be able to think in advance, uh, well, I'm gonna talk about being on Shark Tank because that's always good fodder for interesting conversation and the crazy things that happened that one time I was on TV.
And so somebody says, "What do you do?"
And you might start off by saying, "Well, I'm an entrepreneur, but I have to tell you, I've only had 15 minutes of fame.
My company may not be doing very well right now, but once I was actually on Shark Tank, and I have the craziest stories about Mr. Wonderful."
So you brought up the topic, and you've really served up a interesting menu to your conversation partner about something to talk about right away.
I really like the idea of delineating your authentic differences in your brand as circles that overlap in a Venn diagram.
A lot of people say, "Just list out all the different things," but the physical representation and overlaps is what I think can be really interesting because that is what makes you unique.
There might be a lot of people who have tenacity and a lot of people who have deep knowledge in one area, but that overlap makes it unique, and I like that idea of helping us identify it that way.
And then thinking of yourself as a host or a hostess who has to focus that initial interaction, I really like that as well.
Thank you. Many of us struggle in conversation in general, but the real struggle is that first beginning part, that first 60 seconds.
Do you have advice on how to maximize and set ourselves up to enjoy that beginning part?
I feel like once I get over that hump, it becomes much easier.
You're exactly right, that those first 60 seconds are the worst.
I think taking an improv class is always great because that helps teach you to roll with any situation.
But beyond that, there are two other things that I coach my dating clients on.
So the first thing I tell people to ease that first minute is topic prep.
So to think about in advance, again, you're like an athlete stretching and warming up for the exercises.
Topic prep involves just taking a minute or two before you walk into a conversation.
You're maybe going to a business networking event or on a date or a job interview or even catching up with a friend.
And you pause and think of three things that you're curious to ask in advance.
So if it's a stranger you're meeting, you can Google them or find their Instagram or look for clues in some messages you've had so far for what they might be interested in.
But for example, let's say you looked at their Instagram in advance of somebody you're meeting on a date and you saw that this guy had a photo of himself fly fishing.

So maybe that's one of your three topics that you've prepped in advance, and you are gonna ask how he became interested in fly fishing, and maybe that's gonna lead to a story about how his dad taught him to fly fish, and it was bonding, and that opens up conversation about his family.
So I think being prepared is super important.
There's another really interesting trick that works especially well in almost every situation, and it is a Latin phrase called in medias res.
And in medias res means literally in the middle of things.
So this is where you start a story in the middle.

If you've ever seen a TV show where they start with a robbery in progress, and then the show cuts to a phrase on the screen that says, "Three days earlier," and it hooks the listener to show what led up to that moment.
In conversation, starting a story in the middle is something that you actually did the last time you and I had a phone call.
I don't know if you remember this.
I remember the phone call.
I don't remember this.
As soon as we got on the phone, I said to you something like, "Thanks for accommodating my schedule to talk on a Saturday."
And you said, "There I was, toilet shopping with my mom when the reminder for our meeting popped up on my phone."
And so I was immediately hooked.
Toilet shopping for your mom?
What on earth is the backstory to that?

And you just launched into, in medias res, in the middle of a story, something that was unexpected and intriguing, and it really just helped us get over very quickly those awkward first 60 seconds of small talk.
I'm glad I demonstrated that.
Let's just say it was an explosive situation that needed to be fixed, and we took care of it.
Again, the advice is to do some preparation, even though conversations are spontaneous, to, to take the time to do some preparation.
And that reconnaissance, reflection, and research on the person or people you're interacting with can be really helpful.
And the goal is not to script out the communication, but it's really to find the opening for further conversation, is what I heard you say.
And that, to me, is a very different way of approaching.
So it's not just, "What do I say to start it?"
It's, "What do I say to open up the conversation?"
And I like the idea of starting in the middle.
As somebody who teaches people how to give presentations, that's definitely a technique that can be used, and I like that you apply it to conversation.
I wanna talk about how we did prepare for this interview on that phone call on that Saturday.
You and I had a conversation about handling taboo topics, things like money, religion, sex.
You have some really useful ideas about how to discuss these types of topics, which turn out to be really important as we develop deeper relationships with people.
Can you share some tips and tools to help us talk about topics that might be taboo?
People tend to avoid taboo topics because they're fearful of controversy or having awkward moments.
But I would invite people, as they move away from small talk and start to grow and deepen a relationship with somebody, to reframe taboo topics as really a gateway to deepen connections.
For example, what that looks like is not focusing on the facts of the taboo topic, not, "What do you think about it?
Are you in favor of it or against it?"
Those are facts about a taboo topic like money, sex, or religion.
But really to focus on the stories and emotions behind those topics.
So for example, if we use the taboo topic of money, um, it's always somewhat awkward to talk about money for most people.
So let's say you've been dating somebody for a few weeks or months, and you wanna start assessing if your values align on an important topic like money.
So instead of asking a factual-based question like, "Do you consider yourself frugal with your money, or do you spend lavishly?"
You might ask a question that evokes a story like, "What did your parents teach you about money when you were growing up?"
Or you might ask a question like, "What's the first thing you bought with your own money, and why was that important?"
So here you're getting at the why of what they feel and not a factual black or white answer in terms of whether they align with what you think about the topic.

So even though money is one of these topics that people argue a lot about in marriages, what's important is how you argue, not what you're arguing about, and not whether you're on the same page, but how you resolve conflict when it arises.

Taboo topics and using those to get into storytelling about how someone's belief system was shaped, especially at a young age, is really this kind of gateway to making taboo topics a vehicle for deeper connection.
So several things there that I really like, that talking about topics that can be challenging actually deepen the relationship.
And a great way to do it is through asking questions designed for people to explain why.
Tell stories. Help me understand how you came to this rather than what it is you believe.

We had Wendy De La Rosa on, and we talked a lot about money, and, and she had similar advice, that talking about money in her case, but in all these topics, it's really an act of demonstrating care and concern, and that's what deepens those relationships.
And I love the idea of just soliciting stories from people that allow you then to have, again, deeper conversations.
Really good advice.
Well, Rachel, you've been here before.
You know that before we end, I ask everybody three questions.
One I make up just for you, and two I've been asking people for a long time.
And feel free to repeat what you've said before or come up with different answers from our, your previous visit.
Are you ready for these?
Absolutely. Excellent. As a matchmaker, your clients go out on dates every night all over the world, and the date outcome entirely hinges on them having a good or bad conversation.
How do you evaluate a successful or unsuccessful date when you're not there yourself and you're just listening in to what they tell you?
How do you assess a good conversation?
Oh, I love that question.
The truth is, I have one simple question that I reflect back to them, and I ask them, "What side of you did they bring out?"
So what I'm not asking is information-based questions.
I am not asking, "Did you like them?"
Or, "What information did you learn about them?"
Or, "Was there a spark?"
You know, those are typical questions that your friends might ask you when you get back from a date.
I'm asking, "What side of you did they bring out?" to help me determine if this was a good or bad date.
So if their answer is something like, "He brought out my playful side," or maybe, "She brought out my confident side," then I know it was a successful date.
But if their answer was something more like, "Well, actually, he brought out my insecure side," or, "No, no, she brought out my competitive side," that's when I know it didn't go well.
I really like that question for assessing conversation, not just on dates, but in general.
You know, what part of yourself showed up or was able to be shown off in the conversation?
And I think we can all do that ourselves.
We don't need to just go to somebody who's an expert like you and think about that.
I really like that.
I appreciate that question.
Question number two, who's a communicator that you admire, and why?
I've thought about this since the last time I was on the show, and I'm gonna tell you about a personal friend of mine named Katrina.
And the reason I admire her so much is that she always makes me feel good when I talk to her, and she does two specific things that always make me feel good.
First of all, she has a signature expression that she uses all the time, and the expression is, "It's not lost on me."
So she'll say something like, "It's not lost on me that you have an early morning tomorrow and you didn't cancel our dinner tonight.
I really appreciate that you came out and spent this time with me."
So she's just finding a way to show appreciation, and it makes me feel so good, especially when it's something so minor.
You know, it's not lost on her that I didn't cancel our date.
Like, that's a pretty low bar, but here she is feeling so appreciative.
So I think that expression is something that everybody should use more of.
And then the second thing she does is she leaves a lot of voice notes for me instead of texting me.

And I think this is a really underutilized feature on our phones because it's not only unique from everybody else that's texting you, but it's more personal, and it creates an emotional connection when I hear her voice.
And so I would say 8 out of 10 times that I communicate with her is her leaving me a voice note.
Now, I also appreciate that it's not as intrusive as a phone call because that would be her interrupting something else I'm doing.
But, you know, the voice note is just that beautiful, happy medium where I get personal and emotional connection with her, but it's on my own time when I listen to it.
So I think those two things, appreciation and emotional connection, are really what make her a superstar communicator.
I'll start by saying it's not lost on me that you spent a little time thinking about this deeply, and I appreciate that.
And taking the time to express appreciation and finding a unique way to connect with somebody where your true voice, in the case of a voice memo, comes out, I appreciate that.
Well, the final question, Rachel, what are the first three ingredients that go into a successful communication recipe?
The first ingredient is mood.
I think not enough people think about how they make someone feel when they're talking to them.

And so the idea here is that if somebody says something to you like, "I love to ski," you might respond by saying something like, "Me too," if you're the mirror, or you might respond by saying something factual, a, a question like, "Where's your favorite place to ski?"
That would be a very legitimate response.
But a mood-based response to somebody who says they like to ski is more like saying to them, "Tell me the last time you went skiing and you really loved the day."
And that kind of evokes a time for them when they felt good, and you're invoking a positive memory by asking a question that is focused on them telling a story.

It's promoting connection, and it's not garnering information, but really creating a moment between the two of you where they're affiliating the positive mood they are calling up from their memory with almost, like, conflating it with you because you're the one that's experiencing that with them.
The second ingredient I would say is a acronym I use all the time, which is DBB, don't be boring.
I think not enough people use DBB, don't be boring, as a lens to filter their conversation.
And if you can start to remember that every time you go to answer a question in a conversation, first do a quick check, "Is this boring?"
And if it is, come up with something more interesting because boredom is just the enemy of conversation.
And last, I guess the ingredient I would say is probably vulnerability.
Not just showing the polished version of yourself, but really telling a story that's real and humble, maybe self-deprecating.
You could talk about a challenge you're having.
You could talk about an embarrassing moment.
You could talk about a regret.

And it's not about bringing the mood down or being negative, but really just being aware that the polished version of you where everything's great and you're amazing is a lost opportunity for connection.
All of your three ingredients have to do with connection.

I really like the idea of setting the mood through the things you ask and the interaction you have, and that mood does transfer from if I'm having a good time telling you a story, I'm having a good time with you.
And this notion of as you begin to respond in a conversation, you have choices of what to say.
Choose the option that's less boring.
And then finally, being vulnerable, being authentic, really powerful.
Rachel, like all of our conversations, I learn so much from you.
I really appreciate it.

This notion of thinking first and planning before we go into conversation, considering how we bridge into the topics we want to have, and how we can bring out the best in others and ourselves, really important.
Thank you. Thanks for having me.

So I think being prepared is super important. There's another really interesting trick that works especially well in almost every situation, and it is a Latin phrase called in medias res. And in medias res means literally in the middle of things. So this is where you start a story in the middle. If you've ever seen a TV show where they start with a robbery in progress, and then the show cuts to a phrase on the screen that says, "Three days earlier," and it hooks the listener to show what led up to that moment.

In conversation, starting a story in the middle is something that you actually did the last time you and I had a phone call. I don't know if you remember this. I remember the phone call. I don't remember this. As soon as we got on the phone, I said to you something like, "Thanks for accommodating my schedule to talk on a Saturday." And you said, "There I was, toilet shopping with my mom when the reminder for our meeting popped up on my phone."

And so I was immediately hooked. Toilet shopping for your mom? What on earth is the backstory to that? And you just launched into, in medias res, in the middle of a story, something that was unexpected and intriguing, and it really just helped us get over very quickly those awkward first 60 seconds of small talk. I'm glad I demonstrated that. Let's just say it was an explosive situation that needed to be fixed, and we took care of it.

Again, the advice is to do some preparation, even though conversations are spontaneous, to, to take the time to do some preparation. And that reconnaissance, reflection, and research on the person or people you're interacting with can be really helpful. And the goal is not to script out the communication, but it's really to find the opening for further conversation, is what I heard you say. And that, to me, is a very different way of approaching.

So it's not just, "What do I say to start it?" It's, "What do I say to open up the conversation?" And I like the idea of starting in the middle. As somebody who teaches people how to give presentations, that's definitely a technique that can be used, and I like that you apply it to conversation. I wanna talk about how we did prepare for this interview on that phone call on that Saturday.

You and I had a conversation about handling taboo topics, things like money, religion, sex. You have some really useful ideas about how to discuss these types of topics, which turn out to be really important as we develop deeper relationships with people. Can you share some tips and tools to help us talk about topics that might be taboo? People tend to avoid taboo topics because they're fearful of controversy or having awkward moments.

But I would invite people, as they move away from small talk and start to grow and deepen a relationship with somebody, to reframe taboo topics as really a gateway to deepen connections. For example, what that looks like is not focusing on the facts of the taboo topic, not, "What do you think about it? Are you in favor of it or against it?" Those are facts about a taboo topic like money, sex, or religion.

But really to focus on the stories and emotions behind those topics. So for example, if we use the taboo topic of money, um, it's always somewhat awkward to talk about money for most people. So let's say you've been dating somebody for a few weeks or months, and you wanna start assessing if your values align on an important topic like money. So instead of asking a factual-based question like, "Do you consider yourself frugal with your money, or do you spend lavishly?"

You might ask a question that evokes a story like, "What did your parents teach you about money when you were growing up?" Or you might ask a question like, "What's the first thing you bought with your own money, and why was that important?" So here you're getting at the why of what they feel and not a factual black or white answer in terms of whether they align with what you think about the topic.

So even though money is one of these topics that people argue a lot about in marriages, what's important is how you argue, not what you're arguing about, and not whether you're on the same page, but how you resolve conflict when it arises. Taboo topics and using those to get into storytelling about how someone's belief system was shaped, especially at a young age, is really this kind of gateway to making taboo topics a vehicle for deeper connection.

So several things there that I really like, that talking about topics that can be challenging actually deepen the relationship. And a great way to do it is through asking questions designed for people to explain why. Tell stories. Help me understand how you came to this rather than what it is you believe. We had Wendy De La Rosa on, and we talked a lot about money, and, and she had similar advice, that talking about money in her case, but in all these topics, it's really an act of demonstrating care and concern, and that's what deepens those relationships.

And I love the idea of just soliciting stories from people that allow you then to have, again, deeper conversations. Really good advice. Well, Rachel, you've been here before. You know that before we end, I ask everybody three questions. One I make up just for you, and two I've been asking people for a long time. And feel free to repeat what you've said before or come up with different answers from our, your previous visit.

Are you ready for these? Absolutely. Excellent. As a matchmaker, your clients go out on dates every night all over the world, and the date outcome entirely hinges on them having a good or bad conversation. How do you evaluate a successful or unsuccessful date when you're not there yourself and you're just listening in to what they tell you? How do you assess a good conversation? Oh, I love that question.

The truth is, I have one simple question that I reflect back to them, and I ask them, "What side of you did they bring out?" So what I'm not asking is information-based questions. I am not asking, "Did you like them?" Or, "What information did you learn about them?" Or, "Was there a spark?" You know, those are typical questions that your friends might ask you when you get back from a date.

I'm asking, "What side of you did they bring out?" to help me determine if this was a good or bad date. So if their answer is something like, "He brought out my playful side," or maybe, "She brought out my confident side," then I know it was a successful date. But if their answer was something more like, "Well, actually, he brought out my insecure side," or, "No, no, she brought out my competitive side," that's when I know it didn't go well.

I really like that question for assessing conversation, not just on dates, but in general. You know, what part of yourself showed up or was able to be shown off in the conversation? And I think we can all do that ourselves. We don't need to just go to somebody who's an expert like you and think about that. I really like that. I appreciate that question. Question number two, who's a communicator that you admire, and why?

I've thought about this since the last time I was on the show, and I'm gonna tell you about a personal friend of mine named Katrina. And the reason I admire her so much is that she always makes me feel good when I talk to her, and she does two specific things that always make me feel good. First of all, she has a signature expression that she uses all the time, and the expression is, "It's not lost on me."

So she'll say something like, "It's not lost on me that you have an early morning tomorrow and you didn't cancel our dinner tonight. I really appreciate that you came out and spent this time with me." So she's just finding a way to show appreciation, and it makes me feel so good, especially when it's something so minor. You know, it's not lost on her that I didn't cancel our date.

Like, that's a pretty low bar, but here she is feeling so appreciative. So I think that expression is something that everybody should use more of. And then the second thing she does is she leaves a lot of voice notes for me instead of texting me. And I think this is a really underutilized feature on our phones because it's not only unique from everybody else that's texting you, but it's more personal, and it creates an emotional connection when I hear her voice.

And so I would say 8 out of 10 times that I communicate with her is her leaving me a voice note. Now, I also appreciate that it's not as intrusive as a phone call because that would be her interrupting something else I'm doing. But, you know, the voice note is just that beautiful, happy medium where I get personal and emotional connection with her, but it's on my own time when I listen to it.

So I think those two things, appreciation and emotional connection, are really what make her a superstar communicator. I'll start by saying it's not lost on me that you spent a little time thinking about this deeply, and I appreciate that. And taking the time to express appreciation and finding a unique way to connect with somebody where your true voice, in the case of a voice memo, comes out, I appreciate that.

Well, the final question, Rachel, what are the first three ingredients that go into a successful communication recipe? The first ingredient is mood. I think not enough people think about how they make someone feel when they're talking to them. And so the idea here is that if somebody says something to you like, "I love to ski," you might respond by saying something like, "Me too," if you're the mirror, or you might respond by saying something factual, a, a question like, "Where's your favorite place to ski?"

That would be a very legitimate response. But a mood-based response to somebody who says they like to ski is more like saying to them, "Tell me the last time you went skiing and you really loved the day." And that kind of evokes a time for them when they felt good, and you're invoking a positive memory by asking a question that is focused on them telling a story.

It's promoting connection, and it's not garnering information, but really creating a moment between the two of you where they're affiliating the positive mood they are calling up from their memory with almost, like, conflating it with you because you're the one that's experiencing that with them. The second ingredient I would say is a acronym I use all the time, which is DBB, don't be boring. I think not enough people use DBB, don't be boring, as a lens to filter their conversation.

And if you can start to remember that every time you go to answer a question in a conversation, first do a quick check, "Is this boring?" And if it is, come up with something more interesting because boredom is just the enemy of conversation. And last, I guess the ingredient I would say is probably vulnerability. Not just showing the polished version of yourself, but really telling a story that's real and humble, maybe self-deprecating.

You could talk about a challenge you're having. You could talk about an embarrassing moment. You could talk about a regret. And it's not about bringing the mood down or being negative, but really just being aware that the polished version of you where everything's great and you're amazing is a lost opportunity for connection. All of your three ingredients have to do with connection. I really like the idea of setting the mood through the things you ask and the interaction you have, and that mood does transfer from if I'm having a good time telling you a story, I'm having a good time with you.

And this notion of as you begin to respond in a conversation, you have choices of what to say. Choose the option that's less boring. And then finally, being vulnerable, being authentic, really powerful. Rachel, like all of our conversations, I learn so much from you. I really appreciate it. This notion of thinking first and planning before we go into conversation, considering how we bridge into the topics we want to have, and how we can bring out the best in others and ourselves, really important.

Thank you. Thanks for having me. It was a pleasure as always. Thank you for joining us for another episode of Think Fast, Talk Smart, the podcast. study.one_liner_ko: 매치메이커 레이첼 그린왈드가 스몰토크를 '수비'에서 '공격'으로 바꾸는 법 — 브랜딩과 브릿징, 스토리 중심 질문, 분위기·재미·취약성이라는 세 가지 재료를 알려준다.
summary_ko: 스몰토크를 잘하려면 방어(무난한 답 준비)가 아니라 공격(전략적 설계)으로 넘어가야 한다. 내가 가진 독특한 점으로 이어지는 '다리(bridge)'를 미리 생각해 둔다.
퍼스널 브랜딩은 자랑이 아니라 식당 호스트가 '오늘의 추천 메뉴'를 건네는 것과 같다. 진정성 있는 특징 3가지를 벤다이어그램처럼 겹쳐서 '나만의 조합'을 만든다.
처음 60초를 넘기려면 대화 전에 궁금한 것 3가지를 준비하는 '토픽 프렙'과, 이야기를 중간에서 시작하는 in medias res 기법이 유효하다.
돈·종교·성 같은 금기 주제는 사실이 아니라 배경 이야기와 감정을 묻는 질문으로 풀면 관계를 깊게 하는 통로가 된다. 예: '부모님이 돈에 대해 뭘 가르쳐 주셨어?'
데이트가 잘 됐는지는 '상대가 네 어떤 면을 끌어냈나?'로 판단한다. 존경하는 소통가는 'It's not lost on me'로 감사를 표하고 음성 메모로 감정적 연결을 만드는 친구다.
좋은 소통의 세 재료는 분위기(mood), DBB(Don't Be Boring), 그리고 다듬어진 모습 대신 솔직하고 겸손한 취약성이다.
study.summary_en: This episode is with Rachel Greenwald, a matchmaker and dating coach. Her big idea is that small talk should be offense, not defense. You figure out two or three things that make you memorable, then build a bridge from a basic question like 'How are you?' to one of them. She also suggests prepping a few curious questions and starting a story in the middle to get past the awkward first minute. For taboo topics like money, ask about stories and emotions, not facts. Her three ingredients are mood, don't be boring, and vulnerability. I really liked her question: what side of you did they bring out?

expressions.quote: moving from playing defense to offense
expressions.nuance_ko: 스포츠 비유로, 상황에 끌려가지 않고 전략적으로 주도한다는 뜻. 협상·회의·커리어 이야기에서 자주 쓴다. 'go on the offensive'는 공격적 태도에 가까워 약간 더 강하다.
examples: In tomorrow's meeting, let's stop playing defense and put our own proposal on the table first.
After a rough year, the team finally started playing offense instead of just reacting to complaints.
Honestly, with the landlord, I think you need to play offense and ask for the repairs in writing.

similar.example: Nobody was volunteering, so I took the initiative and booked the venue.
We need to get on the front foot with the press before this story spreads.

expressions.expression: find a bridge out of / bridge into
expressions.quote: find a bridge out of the initial stages of small talk
expressions.meaning_ko: (화제 A에서 B로) 자연스럽게 넘어가는 연결고리를 찾다
expressions.nuance_ko: 대화 전환 기술을 말할 때 쓰는 비유다. 동사로 'bridge into a topic'처럼 써도 되고, 'segue'보다 구어적이고 전략적인 느낌이 있다.
examples: I tried to find a bridge out of the weather chat and into what she actually does for work.
When the call dragged on about logistics, he found a nice bridge into the budget discussion.
Mentioning her dog was a good bridge to talking about our weekend hikes.

similar.example: Let me segue into the next point, which is about hiring.
I tried to steer the conversation toward travel because I knew he'd love it.

expressions.quote: that's always good fodder for interesting conversation
expressions.nuance_ko: 원래 가축 사료라는 뜻이라 '자극이나 화젯거리가 되는 재료'로 쓰일 때 약간 유머러스하다. 'fodder for the rumor mill', 'fodder for jokes'처럼 쓴다.
examples: My disastrous trip to Lisbon is great fodder for dinner parties.
That awkward product launch gave the comedians plenty of fodder.
Don't send that email; it's just fodder for gossip around the office.

similar.example: Her commute is basically endless material for stories.
The new policy gave us a few good talking points for the panel.

expressions.quote: you've really served up a interesting menu to your conversation partner
expressions.nuance_ko: 음식 비유를 이어서 '상대에게 먹기 좋게 차려 주다'는 느낌이다. 뉴스·스포츠에서도 'serve up a surprise'처럼 쓴다. 약간 생동감 있는 구어체다.
examples: The opening speaker served up a great story that got everyone laughing.
The finale served up a twist nobody saw coming.
When you introduce a friend, serve up something fun about them so people have a way in.

similar.example: He loves to dish out advice nobody asked for.
She handed me the perfect opening to bring up the raise.

expressions.quote: once I get over that hump, it becomes much easier
expressions.nuance_ko: 시작 단계나 중간의 가장 힘든 구간을 넘었다는 뜻이다. 'over the hump'만 써서 '고비는 넘겼다'고 말하기도 한다. 'hump day'는 수요일을 뜻한다.
examples: Once we get over the hump of the first week, the new system will feel natural.
Training is brutal for the first month, but after you get over that hump it's fun.
I'm over the hump with this report; the hard analysis is done.

similar.example: I think the team is finally turning the corner after the rough start.
A quick joke helped us break the ice.

expressions.quote: teach you to roll with any situation
expressions.nuance_ko: 계획이 틀어져도 당황하지 않고 적응한다는 긍정적 뉘앙스다. 'roll with the punches'가 관용구이고, 'roll with it'은 일상에서 '그냥 흐름대로 가자'는 뜻으로 쓴다.
examples: Our flight got canceled, but we just rolled with it and spent a day in Osaka.
A good presenter can roll with a tough question without losing the thread.
The plan changed twice this morning, so I'm just rolling with it.

similar.example: I'm happy to go with the flow on where we eat.
In Q&A you have to think on your feet.

expressions.quote: it is a Latin phrase called in medias res
expressions.nuance_ko: 글쓰기·영화·스토리텔링 용어이며 대화에서는 지적인 느낌이 난다. 말할 때는 '이야기를 중간에서 시작한다'고 풀어 쓰는 편이 자연스럽다. 발표 오프닝에도 쓸 수 있다.
examples: I opened my talk in medias res: 'The elevator doors closed, and I realized I had the wrong slides.'
A lot of thrillers start in medias res and then circle back.
When you tell a travel story, start in medias res instead of with 'So we woke up at six.'

similar.example: The show has a cold open before the title sequence.
Let's skip the intro and jump straight into the story.

expressions.quote: the date outcome entirely hinges on them having a good or bad conversation
expressions.nuance_ko: 결과가 하나의 핵심 요소에 좌우된다는 뜻이며 'depend on'보다 결정적이고 약간 격식 있다. 뉴스나 회의에서 자주 쓰며 'it all hinges on X' 형태가 자연스럽다.
examples: The whole deal hinges on whether the landlord signs by Friday.
Our trip hinges on the weather, so let's wait to book.
Her promotion hinges on how the next presentation goes.

similar.example: In the end it comes down to trust.
A lot is riding on this interview.

expressions.quote: What side of you did they bring out?
expressions.nuance_ko: 누군가와 있을 때 어떤 모습이 드러나는지 말할 때 쓴다. 'bring out the best in someone'이 가장 흔한 형태다. 관계·팀 분위기·리더십 이야기에 유용하다.
examples: Honestly, my old manager brought out the best in everyone on the team.
Traffic brings out my worst side.
Traveling with her brings out my adventurous side.

similar.example: A good interviewer knows how to draw out shy candidates.

similar.expression: show someone in a new light
similar.example: The crisis showed her in a whole new light.

expressions.expression: It's not lost on me that...
expressions.quote: It's not lost on me that you have an early morning tomorrow
expressions.meaning_ko: ~라는 걸 잘 알고 있고 고맙게(심각하게) 생각한다
expressions.nuance_ko: 상대의 수고나 상황을 내가 인지한다고 정중하게 인정하는 표현이다. 감사뿐 아니라 'It's not lost on me that this is a sensitive issue'처럼 어려운 사정을 인정할 때도 쓴다. 약간 격식 있는 구어체다.
examples: It's not lost on me that you rearranged your whole week to help with the move.
It's not lost on me that this is a tough time for the team, so I'll keep this short.
It's not lost on me that you drove two hours just to be here. Thank you.

similar.example: I'm well aware that everyone is tired, but this matters.

similar.expression: I don't take it for granted that
similar.example: I don't take it for granted that you showed up.

expressions.nuance_ko: 'set the bar low'의 명사형으로, 기대치나 기준이 낮다고 말할 때 쓴다. 가벼운 자조나 아이러니로도 많이 쓰인다. 반대는 'a high bar'다.
examples: 'Show up on time' is a pretty low bar, and he still missed it.
The restaurant was just okay, but the bar was low after last week.
For a first draft, the bar is low; just get ideas on the page.

similar.example: She set the bar high with her first talk.
Sending a thank-you note is hardly a tall order.

expressions.quote: to reframe taboo topics as really a gateway to deepen connections
expressions.meaning_ko: X를 Y로 재해석하다, 관점을 바꿔 보다
expressions.nuance_ko: 부정적으로 보이는 것을 긍정적 틀로 바꿀 때 쓴다. 코칭·협상·리더십에서 자주 나온다. 'a gateway to'는 '~로 가는 입구'라는 뜻의 같이 쓰이는 표현이다.
examples: Try to reframe the criticism as free coaching.
I started to reframe my commute as my only quiet time of the day.
Let's reframe this problem as a chance to rethink the schedule.

similar.expression: look at X through a different lens
similar.example: Look at the delay through a different lens: it gives us time to test.
He tried to put a positive spin on the bad numbers.

expressions.quote: as a lens to filter their conversation
expressions.nuance_ko: '~라는 렌즈로 걸러서 본다'는 뜻으로, 의사결정 기준을 말할 때 쓴다. 'through the lens of ~'와 함께 알아두면 좋다. 코칭·전략 논의에서 세련되게 들린다.
examples: I use one question as a lens to filter every invitation: will I regret skipping this?
Try using 'would a stranger understand this?' as a lens to filter your slides.
She filters every job offer through the lens of what she'll learn.

similar.example: My litmus test for a good meeting is whether I can summarize it in one line.
My rule of thumb is to avoid replying when I'm angry.

vocab.example: Let's delineate who owns which part of the project before we start.
Her tenacity is the reason we finally got the permit.
He's frugal on groceries but spends freely on travel.
That song evokes summers at my grandparents' house.
People often conflate being busy with being productive.
His self-deprecating humor made the room relax.
I did a bit of reconnaissance on the restaurant before booking.
The voice-message feature is wildly underutilized at most companies.

warmup.q: What is your usual way of handling small talk at a networking event, and how do you feel about it?
warmup.hint_ko: 평소 스몰토크 습관(방어형인지 공격형인지), 불편함, 효과를 있었던 경험과 함께 말하기.

warmup.q: Can you think of a conversation where someone's story really hooked you? What made it work?
warmup.hint_ko: 구체적인 사례, 이야기의 시작 방식, 감정 반응을 설명.

opinion.q: Do you agree that personal branding is just a way of helping others find something to talk about, rather than bragging?
opinion.hint_ko: 자랑과 전략적 자기 소개의 경계, 문화 차이(한국/해외), 본인 경험 언급.

opinion.q: Rachel judges a date by 'What side of you did they bring out?' Would this question work for evaluating a meeting or a colleague?
opinion.hint_ko: 업무 상황에 적용, 어떤 면이 드러날 때 좋은 협업인지, 한계도 언급.

debate.q: Should you prepare topics and bridges in advance for a conversation, or is that inauthentic?
debate.for: Preparation reduces anxiety, makes you memorable, and shows respect for the other person's time. Even athletes warm up before playing.
debate.against: Over-planning can make you sound scripted and distract you from really listening. Authentic chemistry should be spontaneous.

debate.q: Is showing vulnerability early on in professional relationships a strength or a risk?
debate.for: Admitting a regret or an embarrassing moment builds trust fast and makes you more human and memorable.
debate.against: In competitive workplaces it can undermine your credibility, and people may use it against you.

roleplay.scenario: You are at a conference reception and meet a senior person from another company whom you'd like to impress and learn from. You have only a minute or two.
roleplay.your_role: A professional who has prepared three topics and a bridge from basic small talk to something memorable about you.
roleplay.partner_role: A friendly but busy senior executive who tends to give short, polite answers at first.
goals: Use a bridge to move from a basic question to a story that shows your personal brand.
Start one story in medias res and invite the partner to share a story with a mood-based question.
Show appreciation with 'It's not lost on me that...' and end the conversation gracefully.

useful_phrases.phrase: Boredom is the enemy of conversation.
I'm curious how you got into that.
useful_phrases.ko: 어떻게 그 일을 시작하게 됐는지 궁금해요.

useful_phrases.phrase: What did your parents teach you about that growing up?
useful_phrases.ko: 어릴 때 부모님이 그것에 대해 뭘 가르쳐 주셨어요?

useful_phrases.phrase: Tell me about the last time you really loved the day.
useful_phrases.ko: 정말 좋았던 하루가 가장 최근에 언제였는지 얘기해 주세요.

useful_phrases.phrase: It's not lost on me that you made time for this.
useful_phrases.ko: 이 시간을 내 주신 걸 잘 알고 있어요.

useful_phrases.phrase: Let me start in the middle of the story.

shadowing.reason_ko: 'moving from playing defense to offense'처럼 핵심 프레임을 또렷하게 제시하는 구조라 패널·회의에서 개념을 소개하는 리듬을 연습하기 좋다.
'not X, but Y' 대비 구조로 재프레이밍하는 논리 전개가 선명하다. 긴 문장에서도 강세와 끊어 읽기를 연습하기 좋다.
DBB 개념을 짧고 기억에 남게 정리하고 마무리 문장으로 'boredom is just the enemy of conversation'을 던지는 임팩트 있는 구성이다.

difficulty.note_ko: 속도는 보통이고 문장 구조가 명확해 듣기 어렵지 않다. 다만 스포츠·음식 비유와 'hinge on', 'lost on me' 같은 관용적 표현, 라틴어가 섞여 있다. 일상 어휘가 중심이라 바로 따라 쓰기 좋다.

translations_sent.0-0: 대화는 정말 힘들 수 있지만, 약간의 준비와 브리징만 있으면 훌륭한 소통을 할 수 있습니다.
translations_sent.1-1: 저는 맷 에이브러햄스이고, 스탠퍼드 경영대학원에서 전략적 커뮤니케이션을 가르치고 있습니다.
translations_sent.2-2: 팟캐스트 '씽크 패스트, 토크 스마트'에 오신 것을 환영합니다.
translations_sent.3-3: 오늘은 제 친구 레이첼 그린왈드와 또 한 번 대화를 나누게 되어 정말 기쁩니다.
translations_sent.4-4: 레이첼은 하버드 경영대학원의 이그제큐티브 펠로이자 전문 매치메이커, 그리고 데이트 코치입니다.
translations_sent.5-5: 레이첼은 연애 분야뿐만 아니라 직장에서도 소통과 관계 형성에 정통한 전문가입니다.
translations_sent.6-6: 지금은 스탠퍼드 캠퍼스에서 티나 실리그 교수님과 '사랑을 위한 디자인'이라는 수업을 공동으로 가르치고 있습니다.
translations_sent.7-7: 어서 오세요, 레이첼. 다시 와 주셔서 정말 기쁘고, 이번에는 직접 만나서 더 좋네요.
translations_sent.12-12: 자, 지난번에 오셨을 때 스몰토크 얘기를 많이 했는데, 아주 실용적이고 유용한 조언을 해 주셔서 저는 지금도 스몰토크를 시작하고 마무리할 때 그걸 쓰고 있어요.
translations_sent.13-13: 알려 주신 백기 접근법은 정말 훌륭했고, 스몰토크는 흥미로운 사람이 되는 게 아니라 흥미를 가져 주는 것이라는 말씀도 저는 자주 인용해요.
translations_sent.14-14: 그리고 레이첼의 스몰토크 조언이 궁금하신 분은 217화로 돌아가서 들어 보세요.
translations_sent.15-15: 그럼 그게 입문 단계, 초급 수준의 스몰토크 조언과 팁이었다면, 이번에는 고급 조언, 그러니까 검은 띠 수준의 스몰토크 팁을 알려 주실 수 있을까요? 우리가 더 잘 소통하고, 다들 느끼는 그 두려움도 피할 수 있게요.
translations_sent.16-16: 네, 다들 스몰토크를 싫어하죠. 대부분 너무 지루하고 어색하니까요.
translations_sent.17-17: 그래서 대학원 수준의 스몰토크 조언으로 올라간다는 건 결국 수비에서 공격으로 넘어가는 거라고 생각해요.
translations_sent.18-18: 수비는 기본적인 스몰토크 질문에 좋은 답을 준비하는 거예요. 지난번에 얘기했던 것처럼요.
translations_sent.19-19: 반면 공격은 스몰토크를 전략적으로 활용해서, 대화 상대가 여러분에 대해 뭔가를 알게 하고, 그게 여러분이 원하는 목표로 이어지게 하는 거예요.
translations_sent.20-20: 바로 여기서 개인 브랜드가 등장해요. 스몰토크 초반 단계에서 벗어나, 여러분을 독특하고 기억에 남게 만드는 주제로 이어지는 다리를 찾았으면 해요.
translations_sent.22-22: 데이트 중이거나 면접을 보고 있다고 해 볼게요.
translations_sent.23-23: 잘 되길 바라니까 미리 이렇게 생각해 보는 거죠. '이번 주에 그 사람이 만난 다른 데이트 상대들, 혹은 면접 본 다른 지원자들과 비교해서 나를 특별하게 만드는 건 뭘까?'
translations_sent.24-24: 맷의 경우라면, 아마 팟캐스트 진행자라는 점이 독특하겠죠.
translations_sent.26-26: 제가 바라는 건 '어떻게 지내세요?' 같은 기본적인 스몰토크 질문에서 팟캐스트 진행자라는 얘기를 할 수 있는 지점으로 이어 주는 다리를 찾는 거예요.
translations_sent.27-27: 예를 들어 제가 '어떻게 지내세요?' 하고 물으면,
translations_sent.28-28: 이렇게 말할 수 있죠. '아, 오늘 정말 잘 지내요.
translations_sent.29-29: 방금 제 팟캐스트에서 아주 흥미로운 게스트를 인터뷰했는데, 오가닉 와인에 대해 전부 얘기해 주셨거든요.'
translations_sent.30-30: 이제 좀 더 흥미로운 주제로 다리를 놓은 거예요.
translations_sent.31-31: 다만 핵심은 이런 대화에 들어가기 전에 계획이 있어야 한다는 거예요. 즉석에서 그런 말이 떠오르길 기대할 수는 없으니까요.
translations_sent.32-32: 운동선수라고 생각해 보세요. 그냥 갑자기 운동을 시작하지는 않잖아요.
translations_sent.33-33: 운동 전에 스트레칭도 하고 몸도 풀겠죠.
translations_sent.34-34: 이런 예시는 정말 많아요. 예를 들어 면접에서 여러분을 독특하게 만드는 개인 브랜드 특성 중 하나가 끈기 있다는 거라고 해 볼게요.
translations_sent.36-36: 면접관 사무실에 들어갔는데, 그분 뒤쪽 책상 위에 산을 오르는 본인 사진이 놓여 있다고 해 봐요.
translations_sent.37-37: 그러면 이렇게 다리를 놓을 수 있어요. '아, 저쪽에 있는 등산 사진을 봤어요.
translations_sent.38-38: 어디 산인지 궁금하네요. 저도 올해 킬리만자로를 올랐거든요. 정말 힘들었지만 해냈어요.'
translations_sent.39-39: 이렇게 기본적인 스몰토크를 전략적인 대화로 바꿔서 자신의 개인 브랜드, 이 경우엔 근성을 보여 주는 거예요.
translations_sent.40-40: 그러니까 제가 듣기엔 핵심은 브랜딩과 브리징, 그리고 그 둘을 어떻게 연결하느냐네요.
translations_sent.41-41: 그러려면 조금 전략적으로, 나를 독특하게 만드는 게 무엇인지 미리 생각해 둬야 하고요.
translations_sent.42-42: 우리 각자의 개인 브랜드를 돌아볼 때 해 주실 조언이 있을까요?
translations_sent.43-43: 이 프로그램에 세스 고딘과 도리 클락도 나와서 개인 브랜드에 대해 이야기했었죠.
translations_sent.44-44: 그런데 매치메이커로서 우리 모두에게 도움이 될 만한, 브랜드를 바라보는 특별한 방식이 있는지 궁금해요.
translations_sent.45-45: 있어요. 우선 개인 브랜딩에 대해 먼저 말하고 싶은 건, 나를 독특하거나 특별하거나 기억에 남게 하는 걸 이야기하면 조작적이다, 잘난 척이나 과시하는 거다, 이런 식으로 평판이 안 좋다는 거예요.
translations_sent.46-46: 그래서 먼저 그런 생각을 머릿속에서 털어내야 해요. 개인 브랜딩의 더 좋은 비유는 식당에 들어서는 장면이에요. 입구에서 안내 직원이 맞이하는데, 기본적인 스몰토크를 할 수도 있죠. '안녕하세요?
translations_sent.48-48: 아니면 메뉴판을 건네면서 '오늘 저녁 메뉴 중에 어떤 게 맛있어 보이세요?' 하고 말할 수도 있어요.
translations_sent.49-49: 결국 첫인사의 초점을 셰프 추천 요리나 그 식당의 대표 메뉴에 맞추는 거죠.
translations_sent.50-50: 개인 브랜딩에 대한 태도가 바로 잡혔다면, 개인 브랜드가 뭔지 가장 쉽게 파악하는 지름길은 나를 독특하게 만드는 특성이나 기술 세 가지를 떠올리는 거예요.
translations_sent.51-51: 세스 고딘이 『보랏빛 소가 온다』에서 이 얘기를 했죠. 기본적으로 어떻게 독특하고 기억에 남을 수 있는가에 대해서요.
translations_sent.52-52: 저는 진정성 있으면서도 독특하게 느껴지는 것 세 가지를 떠올리면 된다고 생각해요. 나라는 사람의 벤다이어그램에서 독특한 부분이 어디인지 보는 거죠.
translations_sent.53-53: 예를 들어 데이트 중인데, 세 가지 개인 브랜드 특성이 모험을 좋아하고, 한때 샤크 탱크에 출연했고, 노스다코타 출신이라고 해 볼게요.
translations_sent.54-54: 노스다코타 출신이라는 건 뉴욕이나 캘리포니아 출신인 것과는 다르잖아요.
translations_sent.55-55: 독특하죠. 그러니까 그 개인 브랜드의 일부를 골라서, 스몰토크에서 벗어나 기억에 남게 해 주는 주제로 이어 가는 다리를 찾는 거예요.
translations_sent.56-56: 물론 샤크 탱크에 나온 사람이 혼자만은 아닐 수 있고요.
translations_sent.59-59: 하지만 그 세 가지가 겹치는 벤다이어그램의 교집합은 여러분뿐일 수 있고, 데이트 상대가 '무슨 일 하세요?' 하고 물을 때 그게 아주 좋은 출발점이 돼요.
translations_sent.60-60: 미리 이렇게 생각해 둘 수 있겠죠. 음, 샤크 탱크에 나온 얘기를 해야겠다, 그건 항상 재미있는 대화거리가 되니까. 그리고 TV에 나갔던 그때 벌어진 황당한 일들도요.
translations_sent.61-61: 그래서 누가 '무슨 일 하세요?' 하고 물으면,
translations_sent.62-62: 이렇게 시작할 수 있어요. '음, 저는 사업가인데, 솔직히 말씀드리면 15분짜리 유명세를 누려 본 게 전부예요.
translations_sent.63-63: 회사는 지금 별로 잘 안 될 수도 있지만, 사실 한 번 샤크 탱크에 나갔었고, 미스터 원더풀에 대해서는 정말 황당한 얘기들이 있어요.'
translations_sent.64-64: 이렇게 직접 주제를 꺼내서, 대화 상대에게 바로 이야기할 만한 흥미로운 메뉴를 내놓은 거죠.
translations_sent.65-65: 브랜드에서 진짜 나만의 차이점을 벤다이어그램처럼 겹치는 원으로 그려 본다는 아이디어가 정말 마음에 들어요.
translations_sent.66-66: 많은 사람들이 '그냥 이것저것 다 적어 보세요'라고 하는데, 시각적으로 표현해서 겹치는 부분을 보는 게 정말 흥미로울 수 있다고 봐요. 그게 바로 나를 독특하게 만드니까요.
translations_sent.67-67: 끈기 있는 사람도 많고, 한 분야에 깊은 지식이 있는 사람도 많겠지만, 그 둘이 겹치면 독특해지죠. 그런 식으로 파악하도록 도와주는 아이디어가 마음에 들어요.
translations_sent.68-68: 그리고 스스로를 첫 만남의 초점을 잡아 줘야 하는 호스트나 호스티스로 생각하는 것도 정말 좋아요.
translations_sent.69-69: 고마워요. 우리 중 많은 사람이 대화 자체를 어려워하지만, 진짜 어려운 건 맨 처음 그 60초예요.
translations_sent.70-70: 그 초반을 최대한 즐길 수 있게 준비하는 방법에 대한 조언이 있으신가요?
translations_sent.71-71: 그 고비만 넘기면 훨씬 쉬워지는 것 같거든요.
translations_sent.73-73: 즉흥 연기 수업을 듣는 것도 늘 좋아요. 어떤 상황이든 유연하게 받아넘기는 법을 가르쳐 주거든요.
translations_sent.74-74: 하지만 그것 말고도 제가 데이트 고객들에게 코칭하는 두 가지가 있어요.
translations_sent.75-75: 첫 1분을 편하게 만들기 위해 제가 먼저 알려 드리는 건 주제 준비예요.
translations_sent.76-76: 미리 생각해 두는 거죠. 아까 말했듯이, 운동선수가 운동 전에 스트레칭하고 몸을 푸는 것과 같아요.
translations_sent.77-77: 주제 준비는 대화에 들어가기 전에 1~2분만 시간을 내는 거예요.
translations_sent.78-78: 비즈니스 네트워킹 행사에 가거나, 데이트나 면접을 앞두고 있거나, 아니면 친구와 근황을 나누는 자리일 수도 있죠.
translations_sent.79-79: 그럴 때 잠깐 멈춰서 미리 물어보고 싶은 궁금한 것 세 가지를 떠올려 보세요.
translations_sent.80-80: 그러니까 처음 만나는 사람이라면, 구글에서 검색해 보거나 인스타그램을 찾아보거나, 지금까지 주고받은 메시지에서 그 사람이 뭘 좋아할지 단서를 찾아볼 수 있어요.
translations_sent.81-81: 예를 들어 데이트하기 전에 상대의 인스타그램을 봤는데, 그 남자가 플라이 낚시하는 사진을 올려놨다고 해 볼게요.
translations_sent.82-82: 그럼 미리 준비해 둔 세 가지 주제 중 하나가 될 수 있겠죠. 어떻게 플라이 낚시에 관심을 갖게 됐는지 물어보면, 아버지가 플라이 낚시를 가르쳐 주셨고 그게 유대감이 됐다는 이야기로 이어질 수도 있고, 그러면 그 사람의 가족 이야기로 대화가 넓어지는 거죠.
translations_sent.83-83: 그래서 준비하는 게 정말 중요하다고 생각해요.
translations_sent.84-84: 또 하나, 거의 모든 상황에서 특히 잘 통하는 아주 흥미로운 요령이 있는데, 라틴어로 '인 메디아스 레스'라고 해요.
translations_sent.85-85: 인 메디아스 레스는 말 그대로 '일의 한가운데서'라는 뜻이에요.
translations_sent.87-87: 강도 사건이 한창 벌어지는 장면으로 시작했다가 화면에 '3일 전'이라는 자막이 나오면서 그 순간에 이르기까지의 과정을 보여주는 TV 프로그램 본 적 있으시죠? 그렇게 시청자를 확 사로잡는 거예요.
translations_sent.88-88: 대화에서 이야기를 중간부터 시작하는 건, 사실 지난번에 우리가 통화했을 때 당신이 실제로 했던 거예요.
translations_sent.92-92: 전화를 받자마자 제가 "토요일에 통화하게 일정 맞춰 주셔서 감사해요" 비슷한 말을 했어요.
translations_sent.93-93: 그랬더니 당신이 "저는 엄마랑 변기를 사러 갔다가 우리 미팅 알림이 휴대폰에 딱 떴어요"라고 했죠.
translations_sent.97-97: 그렇게 인 메디아스 레스, 그러니까 이야기 한가운데로 불쑥 들어가서 예상 밖이고 흥미로운 이야기를 꺼냈고, 덕분에 어색한 첫 60초의 스몰토크를 아주 빨리 넘길 수 있었어요.
translations_sent.99-99: 폭발적인 상황이라 고쳐야 했고, 그래서 해결했다고만 해 둘게요.
translations_sent.100-100: 다시 말씀드리면, 대화는 즉흥적이지만 시간을 들여 준비를 하라는 게 조언이에요.
translations_sent.101-101: 그리고 대화할 상대에 대해 미리 살펴보고, 생각해 보고, 조사해 두는 게 정말 도움이 될 수 있죠.
translations_sent.102-102: 목표는 대화를 대본처럼 짜는 게 아니라 더 이어갈 수 있는 실마리를 찾는 거라고 제가 이해했어요.
translations_sent.103-103: 그리고 그건 저한테 아주 다른 접근법으로 느껴져요.
translations_sent.106-106: 그리고 중간부터 시작한다는 아이디어가 마음에 들어요.
translations_sent.107-107: 저는 사람들에게 프레젠테이션하는 법을 가르치는 사람인데, 그건 분명히 쓸 수 있는 기법이고, 그걸 대화에 적용하셨다는 점이 좋네요.
translations_sent.108-108: 그 토요일 통화에서 우리가 이 인터뷰를 어떻게 준비했는지 이야기해 보고 싶어요.
translations_sent.109-109: 그때 돈, 종교, 성 같은 금기시되는 주제를 다루는 법에 대해 이야기했죠.
translations_sent.110-110: 이런 주제를 어떻게 이야기할지에 대해 아주 유용한 아이디어를 갖고 계신데, 사람들과 더 깊은 관계를 쌓아갈수록 이게 정말 중요해지거든요.
translations_sent.111-111: 금기시될 수 있는 주제를 이야기하는 데 도움이 될 만한 팁과 도구를 알려주실 수 있나요?
translations_sent.112-112: 사람들은 논란이 되거나 어색해질까 봐 금기 주제를 피하는 경향이 있어요.
translations_sent.113-113: 하지만 저는 스몰토크에서 벗어나 누군가와 관계를 키우고 깊게 만들어 가는 단계에서는, 금기 주제를 관계를 깊게 만드는 관문으로 다시 바라보라고 권해요.
translations_sent.114-114: 예를 들면, 금기 주제의 사실관계에 초점을 맞추지 않는 거예요. "그것에 대해 어떻게 생각해요?
translations_sent.116-116: 그런 건 돈이나 성, 종교 같은 금기 주제에 대한 사실, 즉 입장에 관한 거죠.
translations_sent.117-117: 대신 그 주제 뒤에 있는 이야기와 감정에 초점을 맞춰야 해요.
translations_sent.118-118: 예를 들어 돈이라는 금기 주제를 보면, 음, 대부분의 사람에게 돈 얘기는 늘 좀 어색하죠.
translations_sent.119-119: 가령 몇 주 혹은 몇 달째 누군가와 만나고 있고, 돈처럼 중요한 주제에서 가치관이 맞는지 알아보고 싶다고 해 볼게요.
translations_sent.120-120: 그럴 때 "스스로 돈을 아끼는 편이라고 생각해요, 아니면 펑펑 쓰는 편이에요?" 같은 사실 위주의 질문 대신에
translations_sent.121-121: "어렸을 때 부모님이 돈에 대해 뭘 가르쳐 주셨어요?" 같이 이야기를 끌어내는 질문을 할 수 있어요.
translations_sent.122-122: 아니면 "처음으로 자기 돈으로 산 게 뭐예요? 그게 왜 중요했어요?" 같은 질문도 있고요.
translations_sent.123-123: 이렇게 하면 그 사람이 느끼는 이유에 다가가게 되고, 내 생각과 맞는지 아닌지 같은 흑백의 사실적인 답을 얻는 게 아니에요.
translations_sent.124-124: 돈은 부부들이 많이 다투는 주제 중 하나지만, 중요한 건 무엇을 두고 다투느냐가 아니라 어떻게 다투느냐예요. 같은 생각이냐가 아니라, 갈등이 생겼을 때 어떻게 푸느냐죠.
translations_sent.125-125: 금기 주제를 활용해서, 특히 어린 시절에 그 사람의 신념 체계가 어떻게 형성됐는지 이야기를 나누는 건, 금기 주제를 더 깊은 연결의 수단으로 만드는 관문 같은 거예요.
translations_sent.126-126: 제가 정말 마음에 드는 게 여러 가지 있는데, 어려울 수 있는 주제를 이야기하는 게 오히려 관계를 깊게 한다는 점이 그래요.
translations_sent.127-127: 그리고 그러는 좋은 방법은 사람들이 이유를 설명하도록 질문을 던지는 거고요.
translations_sent.128-128: 이야기를 들려달라고 하는 거죠. 무엇을 믿는지보다 어떻게 그런 생각에 이르렀는지 이해하게 도와달라고요.
translations_sent.129-129: 저희 프로그램에 웬디 드 라 로사가 나왔을 때 돈 이야기를 많이 했는데, 그분도 비슷한 조언을 했어요. 그분은 돈에 대해서였지만 이런 모든 주제에서, 돈 얘기를 하는 건 배려와 관심을 보여주는 행동이고, 그게 관계를 깊게 한다고요.
translations_sent.130-130: 그리고 사람들에게서 이야기를 끌어내서 다시 더 깊은 대화를 나눌 수 있게 한다는 아이디어가 정말 좋아요.
translations_sent.133-133: 마무리하기 전에 제가 모든 게스트에게 세 가지 질문을 하는 거 아시죠.
translations_sent.134-134: 하나는 게스트에 맞게 제가 새로 만들고, 나머지 둘은 오랫동안 계속 해 온 질문이에요.
translations_sent.135-135: 예전에 하신 답을 그대로 말씀하셔도 되고, 지난번과 다른 답을 하셔도 괜찮아요.

translations_sent.138-138: 본인은 그 자리에 없고 고객이 해 주는 얘기만 듣는 상황에서, 데이트가 성공적이었는지 아닌지 어떻게 평가하세요?
translations_sent.141-141: 사실 제가 고객에게 되묻는 간단한 질문이 하나 있어요. "그 사람이 당신의 어떤 면을 끌어냈나요?"라고 물어요.
translations_sent.142-142: 그러니까 제가 묻지 않는 건 정보 위주의 질문이에요.
translations_sent.144-144: "그 사람에 대해 어떤 정보를 알게 됐어요?"라든가
translations_sent.146-146: 그런 건 데이트 갔다 오면 친구들이 흔히 물어보는 질문이잖아요.
translations_sent.147-147: 저는 "그 사람이 당신의 어떤 면을 끌어냈나요?"라고 물어서 이 데이트가 좋았는지 나빴는지 판단해요.
translations_sent.148-148: "장난기 많은 면을 끌어냈어요"라든가 "자신감 있는 면을 끌어냈어요" 같은 대답이면 성공적인 데이트라는 걸 알죠.
translations_sent.149-149: 하지만 "음, 사실 불안한 면을 끌어냈어요"라든가 "아니요, 그 사람 때문에 경쟁심이 나왔어요" 같은 대답이면, 잘 안 풀렸다는 걸 알아요.
translations_sent.150-150: 저는 데이트뿐만 아니라 일반적인 대화를 평가하는 데도 그 질문이 정말 좋다고 생각해요.
translations_sent.151-151: 그러니까 대화에서 내 어떤 면이 드러났는지, 또는 어떤 면을 보여줄 수 있었는지를 보는 거죠.
translations_sent.152-152: 그건 우리 모두가 스스로 할 수 있다고 생각해요.
translations_sent.153-153: 꼭 당신 같은 전문가를 찾아가서 생각해야 하는 건 아니죠.
translations_sent.156-156: 두 번째 질문입니다. 존경하는 커뮤니케이터는 누구고, 왜 존경하세요?
translations_sent.157-157: 지난번 출연 이후로 이걸 생각해 봤는데, 제 개인적인 친구인 카트리나 이야기를 할게요.
translations_sent.158-158: 제가 그 친구를 그렇게 존경하는 이유는, 그 친구와 이야기하면 항상 기분이 좋아지기 때문이에요. 그리고 그 친구는 저를 항상 기분 좋게 만드는 구체적인 행동 두 가지를 해요.
translations_sent.159-159: 우선, 그 친구에게는 늘 쓰는 대표적인 표현이 있는데, 바로 "그냥 지나치지 않았어요"라는 말이에요.
translations_sent.160-160: 그래서 그분은 이런 식으로 말해요. "내일 아침 일찍 일정이 있는데도 오늘 저녁 약속을 취소하지 않았다는 걸 내가 모르는 게 아니에요.
translations_sent.161-161: 나와 이렇게 시간을 내서 만나줘서 정말 고마워요."
translations_sent.162-162: 그러니까 그냥 고마움을 표현하는 방법을 찾는 건데, 그게 제 기분을 정말 좋게 해요. 특히 이렇게 사소한 일일 때요.
translations_sent.163-163: 제가 데이트를 취소하지 않았다는 걸 그분은 알아주는 거예요.
translations_sent.164-164: 사실 그건 꽤 낮은 기준이잖아요. 그런데도 그분은 이렇게 진심으로 고마워하는 거죠.
translations_sent.165-165: 그래서 저는 이런 표현을 모든 사람이 더 많이 써야 한다고 생각해요.
translations_sent.166-166: 그리고 두 번째로, 그분은 문자 대신 음성 메시지를 많이 남겨요.
translations_sent.167-167: 이게 우리 휴대폰에서 정말 덜 활용되는 기능이라고 생각하는데, 문자 보내는 다른 사람들과 차별화될 뿐만 아니라 더 개인적이고, 그분 목소리를 들을 때 정서적인 유대감이 생기거든요.
translations_sent.168-168: 그래서 제가 그분과 소통하는 열 번 중 여덟 번은 그분이 음성 메시지를 남기는 거라고 할 수 있어요.
translations_sent.169-169: 또 전화처럼 방해가 되지 않는다는 점도 좋아요. 전화는 제가 하던 다른 일을 끊고 들어오는 거니까요.
translations_sent.170-170: 그런데 음성 메시지는 딱 아름답고 기분 좋은 절충안이에요. 그분과 개인적이고 정서적인 유대감을 느끼면서도, 제가 듣는 건 제 시간에 맞춰서 하니까요.
translations_sent.171-171: 그래서 이 두 가지, 그러니까 고마움 표현과 정서적 유대감이 그분을 최고의 소통가로 만든다고 생각해요.
translations_sent.172-172: 먼저 말씀드리면, 이 문제를 깊이 생각하는 데 시간을 쓰셨다는 걸 제가 모르지 않고, 그래서 감사해요.
translations_sent.173-173: 그리고 시간을 들여 고마움을 표현하고, 음성 메모처럼 진짜 목소리가 드러나는 독특한 방식으로 누군가와 연결되는 방법을 찾는 것, 그 점이 참 좋네요.
translations_sent.174-174: 자, 마지막 질문입니다, 레이첼. 성공적인 소통 레시피에 들어가는 첫 세 가지 재료는 무엇인가요?
translations_sent.176-176: 많은 사람들이 상대와 이야기할 때 자신이 상대방을 어떤 기분이 들게 하는지 충분히 생각하지 않는다고 생각해요.
translations_sent.177-177: 그러니까 누군가 "나는 스키 타는 걸 좋아해요"라고 말하면, 거울형이라면 "저도요"라고 답할 수도 있고, 아니면 "스키 타기 제일 좋은 곳이 어디예요?" 같은 사실적인 질문으로 답할 수도 있어요.
translations_sent.179-179: 하지만 스키를 좋아한다는 사람에게 분위기 중심으로 답한다면 이런 식이에요. "마지막으로 스키 탔을 때 정말 좋았던 날에 대해 얘기해 주세요."
translations_sent.180-180: 그러면 상대가 기분 좋았던 때를 떠올리게 되고, 이야기를 들려달라는 질문으로 긍정적인 기억을 불러일으키는 거예요.
